metaDescription: Six mid-tier universal remotes compared on backlighting, rechargeable power, multi-device control, streaming hotkeys and how much setup each one needs.
introParagraphs: Moving up a tier from the bargain-bin remotes buys real conveniences: backlit keys, a rechargeable battery, streaming hotkeys and control of up to four devices. This page covers six remotes that sit in that middle band, from a rechargeable GE model to simple infrared replacements for Samsung and multi-brand TVs. We evaluated them on device reach, setup, key lighting, power source and how clearly each listing states its limits.

The practical question at this level is whether the extra features match how you actually watch. A backlight is wonderful in a dim living room and irrelevant in a bright one. Four-device control is valuable for a cable box, soundbar and Blu-ray player, and wasted if the TV is the only thing you ever operate.

Several picks here can also be programmed with printed code lists, so expect a short setup session. The simpler infrared replacements skip that step but cover fewer brands, which is the central tradeoff running through this comparison.

products.name: GE Rechargeable Backlit Universal TV Remote

specList.label: Power
specList.value: Rechargeable lithium polymer, lasts months per listing

products.description:
This GE remote swaps disposable batteries for a built-in lithium polymer cell that the listing says stays powered for months on a single charge. It also adds backlit keys, which makes it the most dark-room friendly pick in the group. Dedicated hotkeys reach Netflix, Disney+, Prime Video and YouTube, provided those apps are installed by the TV maker.

It operates up to four devices, including TVs, Blu-ray and DVD players, streaming players, soundbars, cable boxes and satellite receivers. That breadth is the clearest reason to pay for the upper end of this budget. If your cabinet holds more than a TV and a set-top box, this remote consolidates the pile.

The drawback is routine. A rechargeable battery means you must remember to charge it, and a dead remote on movie night is a worse failure than a dead AAA you can swap. Compared with the GE Backlit Universal Remote, which uses two AAA cells, you gain convenience but lose instant battery swaps. Against the Angrox, you gain device reach and lose nothing in layout, so for most buyers with several boxes this is the strongest all-rounder.
products.bestFor: Living rooms with several devices and a habit of watching in the dark.

Backlit keys help in dim rooms
Controls up to four audio and video devices
Hotkeys reach four major streaming apps
cons: Hotkeys work only if the TV supports them
No instant battery swap in an emergency

products.name: Angrox Universal TV Remote Control

specList.label: Brands named
specList.value: Samsung, Vizio, LG, Hisense, TCL, Philips, Sony

specList.label: Exclusions
specList.value: TV sticks, cubes, Roku streaming devices

products.description:
The Angrox pitches itself as a single remote with great value and no setup. It names Samsung, Vizio, LG, Hisense, TCL, Philips and Sony smart TVs, and adds one-click hot keys for Netflix, Prime Video, Disney+ and Hulu so you skip the home-screen hunt.

Those hotkeys are the main appeal. Most budget universals give you a power key and a number pad, while this model lays streaming shortcuts on the face of the remote. The listing is blunt about exclusions: it does not control Roku streaming sticks, any TV sticks or TV cubes, so a Fire Stick or Chromecast needs its own remote.

The tradeoff is scope and resilience. You get TV control only, with no multi-device reach and no backlight. It is simpler than the LOUTOC model that lists DVDs, soundbars and set-top boxes, yet quicker to live with because there is no code list. It also trails the GE Rechargeable on device count. If streaming is how your household watches and a TV is the only device, it is an efficient match.
products.bestFor: Streaming-first households with one smart TV and no extra boxes.

products.description:
LOUTOC's multi-brand remote has the widest device list on paper. Beyond TVs from Samsung, LG, Hisense, TCL, Vizio, Sony, Onn and Toshiba, the listing names DVD and Blu-ray players, soundbars, streaming media players, set-top boxes, DVRs and even VCRs.

Setup uses a code list. You find your brand in the printed table, hold SETUP until the red light comes on, then key in the code. It is a few minutes of work, and nothing here will do it for you automatically. Once configured, a single remote can stand in for several originals.

Its weakness is polish. There are no hotkeys, no backlight and no rechargeable option, so you are paying for reach rather than comfort. Next to the GE Universal Remote it matches the idea of multi-device control but with a longer legacy-device list. Compared with the Angrox, you give up streaming shortcuts and gain flexibility. Keep the code sheet and write the working code on the back, since a battery change can mean starting over.

products.name: EONCHARM Samsung Replacement Remote
products.description:
The EONCHARM is a purpose-built stand-in for a Samsung original. The listing says it works with Samsung LCD, LED, HDTV, 3D and Smart sets, and it names model years running from 2017 through 2024. There is no programming at all, so you add batteries and aim it at the TV.

The design is small with a grip that is meant not to slip, which suits a smaller hand or a drawer-sized spare. It is meant to be the easiest route when an original remote has been dropped, lost or chewed by a pet, and it asks nothing of you beyond confirming your Samsung series.

The tradeoff is that it is only a Samsung remote. The Angrox and LOUTOC picks work across brands, and the GE Backlit model controls up to four devices. If you ever replace the TV with another make, this remote will not follow. For a household committed to one Samsung set, though, it removes the code-list step entirely and matches or beats multi-brand picks on simplicity.

products.name: GE Universal Remote for Samsung, LG, Roku TV

specList.label: Brands named
specList.value: Samsung, LG, Roku TV, Vizio, Sony, Philips, Sharp

products.description:
GE's universal remote handles up to four audio and video devices, including TVs, Blu-ray and DVD players, cable or satellite receivers and soundbars. Its TV button comes preprogrammed for Samsung, so a Samsung owner can start with only a battery change. It also supports Roku TVs and brands such as LG, Vizio, Sony, Philips and Sharp.

The listing credits a large code library covering thousands of recent audio and video devices. For someone with a TV, receiver and Blu-ray player, that library is the draw. The base model carries no backlight, which is its clearest gap against the pricier GE variants.

Ownership is straightforward. You add two AAA batteries, which are not included, and use code search or direct entry for non-Samsung gear. It offers more device reach than the single-purpose EONCHARM and the same four-device count as the GE Rechargeable, minus the charging and lights. Choose it when you want a trusted maker's code library and do not care about night-time visibility.

products.name: GE Backlit Universal Remote Control

specList.label: Setup
specList.value: Automatic code search or direct code entry

specList.label: Brands named
specList.value: Samsung, Vizio, TCL, Hisense, Sony, RCA, Panasonic, Roku, Apple TV

products.description:
The GE Backlit remote adds an illuminated keypad to the familiar four-device GE formula. It names a long run of brands, including Samsung, Vizio, TCL, Hisense, Sony, RCA, Panasonic, Roku and Apple TV, and the listing points to a large code library for current audio and video gear.

Setup offers automatic code search or direct code entry, plus master volume control. You supply two AAA batteries. The glow behind the keys is the reason to choose it over the plain GE Universal model, since you can find volume and input in a dark room without a lamp.

It uses disposable cells where the GE Rechargeable has a built-in battery, so you can swap and keep going, but you will replace them over time. Against the Angrox it gives up streaming hotkeys and gains device reach. As a cheaper route to backlighting than a rechargeable model, it is the most balanced buy in this tier for a household that reads the keypad after sunset.
products.bestFor: Dim living rooms where reading keys without a lamp matters.

buyingCriteria.explanation: A lit keypad changes how a remote feels after sunset, because you stop guessing at volume and input keys. The GE Rechargeable and GE Backlit remotes both include it, while the GE Universal remote explicitly lacks it. If you watch mostly in the evening, treat backlight as a primary requirement and not a luxury. If your living room is bright all day, the plain GE Universal remote or the Angrox gives you the same control for less complexity.

Rechargeable power removes disposable cells, but it adds a charging habit. The GE Rechargeable lists a lithium polymer battery that lasts months between charges, while the GE Backlit and GE Universal take two AAA batteries each. Choose rechargeable if you forget to buy batteries and are happy to plug in a remote every few months. Choose AAA if you want instant swaps and a spare pack in the drawer.

Device count drives the whole price tier, since single-TV remotes are cheap and four-device remotes are not. The GE Rechargeable, GE Universal and GE Backlit each control up to 4 devices, while the Angrox and EONCHARM stay focused on the TV. Count your boxes before buying and add one for anything you might buy in a year. If you have three or more, a four-device model pays for itself in fewer originals on the table.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Look for app hotkeys that fit
buyingCriteria.explanation: Streaming keys save steps but only help if they match your services. The GE Rechargeable lists Netflix, Disney+, Prime Video and YouTube, and the Angrox lists Netflix, Prime Video, Disney+ and Hulu. Check the apps you actually use, because a key for a service you do not subscribe to is dead weight. Remember that on the GE model the hotkeys depend on the TV maker installing the app.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Read the exclusions in the listing
buyingCriteria.explanation: Universal does not mean everything. The Angrox excludes Roku streaming sticks, TV sticks and cubes, and the GE Universal listing notes certain devices are not supported. Look for an explicit exclusion list, since honest listings are the easier ones to trust. If a remote is silent on exclusions, assume a mismatch is possible and keep the return window in mind.

Setup ranges from none to a printed code table. The EONCHARM needs no programming and the Angrox claims no setup, while the LOUTOC requires you to hold SETUP until the red light comes on and key in a code. The GE models offer automatic code search for those who dislike manual lists. Pick no-setup for one TV and code-based remotes only when you need to reach older or additional devices.

howWeEvaluated.title: Device reach
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted how many devices each remote can control and which kinds the listing names. The GE Rechargeable, GE Universal and GE Backlit each manage four devices, the LOUTOC lists the longest set of legacy gear, and the Angrox and EONCHARM stay TV-only. Remotes with explicit exclusions were scored fairly for transparency.

howWeEvaluated.title: Convenience features
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed backlighting, rechargeable power and streaming hotkeys together, since each solves a different annoyance. The GE Rechargeable leads by combining backlighting and rechargeable power, the GE Backlit follows with lighting only, and the Angrox leads on hotkey variety. Features were scored on what the product page states.

howWeEvaluated.title: Setup burden
howWeEvaluated.description: Each pick was scored on how much work stands between the box and a working TV. The EONCHARM and Angrox need little or none, the GE models offer code search, and the LOUTOC asks for the most manual entry. This is based on specs and buyer feedback, not on timed trials.

howWeEvaluated.title: Compatibility clarity
howWeEvaluated.description: A good listing names brands and states what it cannot do. The Angrox and GE Universal listings are explicit about exclusions, and the EONCHARM names model years from 2017 through 2024. Vague listings lost points because they raise the odds of a mismatch.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value inside the cap
howWeEvaluated.description: At the middle tier, the question is what the extra spend buys over a bare replacement. The GE Rechargeable and GE Backlit add comfort, the LOUTOC adds range, and the EONCHARM adds simplicity for Samsung homes. The picks closest to the cap were expected to bring tangible extras.

cards.label: Rechargeable
cards.text: A built-in lithium polymer battery is charged by cable and the GE Rechargeable Backlit Universal TV Remote lists months of use per charge. It saves a stock of cells and suits people who dislike buying batteries. Choose it if you are happy with a charging habit.

cards.label: Battery-powered
cards.text: The GE Backlit Universal Remote Control, GE Universal Remote for Samsung, LG, Roku TV, Angrox, LOUTOC and EONCHARM remotes run on replaceable cells. You can swap instantly and never wait for a charge. Choose this if the remote is shared by people who would forget to plug it in.

howToChoose.note: If one failed charge would annoy the household, the battery side is safer.

faq.q: Is a rechargeable universal remote worth it?
faq.a: It is worth it if you dislike buying batteries and can build a charging habit. The GE Rechargeable lists months of use per charge, which means a few plug-ins a year. The tradeoff is that a dead remote cannot be fixed with a drawer battery. If you share the remote with someone who forgets, take AAA models.

faq.q: Do backlit keys drain the battery faster?
faq.a: They can use a little more power, since the lighting draws current. On the GE Backlit remote, you supply two AAA batteries and should expect to replace them on a normal cycle. The listing does not publish a battery life figure, so treat the lights as a small cost for night-time usability.

faq.q: Can I use these with a Roku stick or Fire Stick?
faq.a: Not reliably. The Angrox listing says it does not control Roku streaming sticks or any TV sticks or cubes. The GE Universal listing notes certain devices are unsupported. Keep the stick's own remote or use its phone app alongside the universal remote.

faq.q: Which pick is best for older equipment?
faq.a: The LOUTOC remote lists DVD and Blu-ray players, DVRs, set-top boxes and VCRs alongside soundbars and streaming players. Its code-list setup takes a few minutes. The GE models also reach older gear through their code libraries, but they do not spell out VCR support as plainly.

faq.q: Are hotkeys the same on every TV?
faq.a: No. A hotkey sends a command that the TV must understand, and the GE Rechargeable listing says its app buttons work when the apps are installed by the TV manufacturer. On a different brand the key may do nothing. Check the app list against what your TV actually has.

faq.q: Why does my code stop working after a battery change?
faq.a: Programmable remotes can lose a stored code if power is missing for long. Write the working code on the back of the remote or on the code sheet. Remotes with no programming, such as the EONCHARM, avoid the issue entirely.

faq.q: What does a higher budget add beyond these picks?
faq.a: Higher tiers add touchscreens, app control, voice search and learning functions. None of these six picks offer those. For most households the four-device GE models with lighting already cover the practical needs, so upgrade only for a feature you can name.
